hook: Hundreds of models. **Five questions** to pick the right one — every single time.

scenes.title: Frontier, open-weight, small — **three families**
scenes.sub: Not 'which is best' — which is best for THIS
scenes.narration: The landscape sorts into three families. Frontier models — the flagships from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google — highest capability, API-only, priced per token. Open-weight models — Llama, Mistral, Qwen — downloadable, runnable on your hardware, fine-tunable. Small models — mini and nano variants — cheap, fast, surprisingly capable, and the first choice for high-volume or on-device work. An architect doesn't ask which model is best; they ask which family fits the constraints.

cards.s: Max capability, zero ops. Data leaves your network; per-token pricing.
Control + privacy + fine-tuning. You own the GPU bill and the uptime.

scenes.narration: The eternal trade. Frontier APIs: the model is better and someone else runs it — but your data crosses a boundary and every token costs money at scale. Self-hosted open-weight: privacy, customization, predictable infrastructure cost — but you become an ML ops team. Many real systems use both: frontier for hard reasoning, small open models for bulk work. That hybrid is a legitimate architecture, not indecision.

scenes.title: Reasoning models **think before they speak**
scenes.sub: Visible chain-of-thought — slower, pricier, sharper at hard problems
scenes.narration: A newer family split: reasoning models — OpenAI's o-series, DeepSeek-R1, and similar — generate internal chain-of-thought before answering. They explore, backtrack, verify. Result: dramatically better at math, code, and multi-step logic. Cost: they use far more tokens thinking, so they're slower and more expensive, and their thinking can still go wrong. Standard models answer directly — faster, cheaper, fine for most language tasks.

items.s: Math proofs, complex code changes, planning with many constraints

items.t: Use standard for: language at speed
items.s: Classification, summarization, extraction, chat — 90% of production traffic
The emerging pattern: cheap model first, escalate to reasoning on failure

scenes.narration: Decision rules. Multi-step logic, code architecture, anything you'd whiteboard — reasoning earns its tokens. High-volume language work — classification, extraction, chat — standard models at a tenth of the cost. And the pattern to steal: model routing. Start every request on the cheap model; only escalate to the expensive thinker when the task proves hard. This one pattern halves AI bills in production.

scenes.title: Text is just **one input** now
scenes.sub: Vision-in, audio-in/out, documents — models have senses
scenes.narration: Multimodal models take more than text. Vision: images, screenshots, charts — describe, extract, answer questions about them. Documents: PDFs go in as pages and come out as understood structure. Audio: speech in and out. For you, the immediate wins are document understanding — invoices, contracts, diagrams — and UI automation from screenshots. One model, several senses, one API shape.

items.s: Send a base64 image or URL alongside the text prompt
Layouts, tables, forms — far beyond naive text extraction
Transcription and voice responses in the same family of models

scenes.narration: Practical entry points. Images ride along in the messages array as base64 or a URL. PDFs — drop them in and ask structured questions; this replaces whole OCR pipelines for many use cases. Audio support varies by model and API — check current docs, this moves fast. Architect's take: multimodality collapses point solutions. The 'separate OCR service', the 'chart parser' — often one vision-capable call now.

scenes.title: Four axes: **quality, cost, latency, privacy**
scenes.sub: Pick the point on the grid — and write down why
scenes.narration: Model selection is a four-axis decision. Quality: does it solve THIS task well — benchmark it on YOUR data, not on marketing charts. Cost: price per token times your volume, plus hidden costs like retries and long outputs. Latency: time to first token for interactive, total time for batch. Privacy: does data leave your network, and is that allowed. Score your top two candidates on your own fifty examples. The answer is usually boring — and that's good.

items.s: 50–100 real examples, blind comparison, measure accuracy — not vibes
(prompt+output tokens × price) × volume — small models win bulk work
Interactive UX needs fast first tokens; batch jobs need cheap totals

scenes.narration: The playbook. First: build a small eval set from real traffic — fifty examples is enough to rank models for your task. Second: do the multiplication — tokens per call, calls per month, price per million; the cheap model often wins by ten times at equal accuracy. Third: separate interactive from batch workloads; they optimize opposite axes. Write the decision and the reason in an architecture note. Future you will thank present you.

scenes.title: Hallucination is a **feature of the design**
scenes.sub: Confident, fluent, wrong — unless you anchor it
scenes.narration: Every LLM hallucinates: fluent, confident, plausible — and fabricated. It's not a bug to be fixed in a future version; it's a consequence of how they work. The model predicts plausible text, it doesn't look things up. So the architecture must supply what the model lacks: retrieval for facts, schemas for structure, validators for values, and humans for judgment. Your job as an architect is not to trust the model — it's to design systems where being wrong is caught.

items.t: Ground it: retrieval over your data
items.s: RAG (Stage 4) gives the model facts to quote instead of invent
Structured output (GA-04) + Pydantic (PY-09) stop shape AND value errors

items.t: Judge it: humans in the loop
items.s: High-stakes outputs get review — diff-approve UIs, not auto-apply

scenes.narration: The three-layer defense. Anchor: give the model real documents to work from — hallucination drops sharply when the answer is in the context. Constrain: schemas force structure, validators force values, and 'I don't know' can be a required field. And for anything that spends money or changes records — a human approves. This is why the capstone agent in this course has an approval step. Design for the model being wrong, and it will rarely hurt you.

scenes.title: Picked a model? Now call it properly
scenes.next: Reel 12 · API Basics — messages, streaming, tokens, rate limits

recap: Three families: frontier API / open-weight self-run / small cheap — hybrid architectures are normal
Reasoning models for hard logic, standard for bulk language work; route and escalate
Hallucination is structural — anchor (retrieval), constrain (schema), judge (humans)

quiz.q: When should you escalate from a standard model to a reasoning model?
opts: For every request — reasoning is always better
Only for multi-step logic where the extra thinking tokens pay off
Never — reasoning models are a gimmick
quiz.why: Reasoning models are slower and costlier (thinking tokens); use them where step-by-step logic matters, not for bulk language work.

quiz.q: What's the most reliable way to compare two models for YOUR use case?
opts: Run both on 50-100 of your own real examples and measure
Ask the models which is smarter
quiz.why: Public benchmarks measure average behavior on generic tasks; your eval set measures the only thing that matters — accuracy on your workload.

quiz.q: Why can't you simply 'fix' hallucination with a better prompt?
opts: Because plausibility is how they're built — the fix is architectural (retrieval, schemas, validators)
Because prompts can't be longer than 100 words
quiz.why: Models generate plausible text rather than verified facts; only external grounding (RAG), enforced structure, and validation actually reduce wrong output.

code.title: A pragmatic model-selection harness
code.body:
import time, json
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

# Your real examples — 50 is enough to rank candidates
EVAL_SET = [
    {"input": "Extract the total from: 'Invoice total: $1,240.00'", "expect": "1240.00"},
    {"input": "Is this refund request abusive? 'give me my money back now!!!'", "expect": "no"},
]

CANDIDATES = ["gpt-4o-mini", "gpt-4o"]   # + your open-weight endpoint

def run(model: str, prompt: str) -> str:
    t0 = time.time()
    r = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=model, temperature=0, max_tokens=80,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )
    ms = (time.time() - t0) * 1000
    usage = r.usage
    return r.choices[0].message.content, ms, usage

for model in CANDIDATES:
    correct, cost, lat = 0, 0.0, []
    for ex in EVAL_SET:
        out, ms, u = run(model, ex["input"])
        correct += ex["expect"] in out
        lat.append(ms)
        # cost += tokens × model price  (fill from the current pricing page)
    print(f"{model}: {correct}/{len(EVAL_SET)}  "
          f"avg {sum(lat)/len(lat):.0f}ms")

# Architect's take: keep this harness. Re-run it whenever you
# consider switching models — decisions become data, not debates.
annot: temperature=0 in evals — you measure the model, not the sampling luck
Track accuracy AND latency AND cost — a model can win two axes and lose the third
Store results per model version; 'gpt-4o' behavior drifts over time

notes:
# Model Landscape

## Three families
| Family | Examples | Strength | Cost shape |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Frontier API | GPT/Claude/Gemini flagships | Max capability | per-token |
| Open-weight | Llama, Mistral, Qwen | privacy, fine-tune, self-run | your GPU |
| Small | *-mini / *-nano | cheap, fast, bulk work | per-token, tiny |

> Hybrid (frontier for hard + small for bulk) is a legitimate architecture.

## Reasoning vs standard
- **Reasoning**: visible chain-of-thought → math, code, multi-step planning. Slower + pricier.
- **Standard**: direct answers → classification, extraction, chat.
- Pattern: **route** — cheap first, escalate on failure.

## Multimodal
- Vision (images/screenshots/charts), PDF understanding, audio.
- Collapses point solutions (OCR, chart parsers) into one call.

## Selection: quality · cost · latency · privacy
- Eval on **your** 50-100 examples · cost math × volume · latency budget per UX type.
- Write the decision + reason in an architecture note.

## Hallucination — a structural property
- Models generate *plausible* text; they don't look things up.
- Defense in depth: **anchor** (RAG) → **constrain** (schema/validators) → **judge** (human-in-loop).
